title: AI Unlocked: Medicine
blurb: For medical students, physicians, and clinical teams: safe clinical prompting, documentation scribes, decision-support and research tools compared head-to-head, imaging frontiers, and a mentor-reviewed clinical AI workflow. 8 in-depth modules, 80 board-style MCQs, printable certificate.

modules.d: The evidence, the economics, and the honest limits of AI in medicine.
modules.body:
Why this course exists

Medicine is in a documented crisis of time. Studies across health systems consistently find physicians spending roughly two hours on the electronic health record and desk work for every one hour of direct patient care, with "pajama time" — after-hours charting — a leading driver of burnout. Meanwhile the biomedical literature doubles at a pace no human can read: PubMed indexes well over a million new citations per year. Into this gap arrives a technology that is genuinely good at exactly the tasks consuming clinicians: transcribing, summarizing, drafting, retrieving, and translating. The clinicians who thrive in the next decade will not be replaced by AI — they will be the ones who direct it with skill and skepticism. This course builds that skill and that skepticism in equal measure.

Cardiologist Eric Topol argues in Deep Medicine that AI’s greatest gift to medicine may be restoring its human side — returning time and presence to the clinician-patient bond. The WHO agrees on the condition: its guidance holds that AI offers "great promise" for health only where ethics and human oversight govern design. That double conviction — leverage plus guardrails — runs through all eight modules.

A working taxonomy: four kinds of medical AI

Confusion about "AI in medicine" usually comes from lumping four very different things together. Keep them separate and every headline becomes easier to judge:

  • 1. Generative assistants (LLMs): ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and their medical derivatives. They generate text: notes, letters, explanations, differentials-as-text. They are trained on the human record, not connected to truth — brilliance and hallucination come from the same mechanism.
  • 2. Ambient documentation (scribes): systems that listen to the visit with consent and draft the clinical note. Narrow, mature, and already deployed at scale across major health systems.
  • 3. Regulated diagnostic devices: FDA-cleared (and internationally approved) algorithms in imaging, cardiology, ophthalmology, pathology. These are medical devices with defined intended uses, validation studies, and failure modes — closer to a CT scanner than to a chatbot.
  • 4. Predictive/operational models: sepsis early-warning scores, no-show predictors, bed-management forecasts. Live inside health systems, largely invisible to patients, and the source of most cautionary tales about bias and drift.

What the evidence actually shows (state of play)

  • Documentation: peer-reviewed evaluations and large health-system deployments of ambient scribes report meaningful reductions in after-hours charting and burnout scores, with note quality rated equal or better after clinician editing. This is the most robust value case in clinical AI today.
  • Knowledge questions: frontier LLMs now pass USMLE-style examinations comfortably and, in blinded studies, their written answers to patient questions have been rated as more complete and — uncomfortably — more empathetic than rushed human replies. Passing an exam is not practicing medicine; it is, however, a real capability signal.
  • Imaging: in screening mammography, large prospective European studies have shown AI-supported reading can maintain or improve cancer detection while cutting radiologist workload substantially. Diabetic retinopathy screening systems operate autonomously at the point of care under regulatory clearance.
  • Cautionary record: a landmark analysis of a widely used commercial risk algorithm found it systematically under-referred Black patients because it used healthcare cost as a proxy for healthcare need — a bias lesson every clinician should be able to recount. Similarly, a widely deployed proprietary sepsis model was found in external validation to miss a large fraction of sepsis cases while generating heavy alert burdens. External validation matters.

The honest limits — memorize these five

  • Hallucination: LLMs generate plausible falsehoods — fabricated citations, invented drug doses, confident wrong facts — because they predict text rather than retrieve truth.
  • Training cutoff and drift: models don’t know last month’s guideline change unless connected to live sources.
  • Distribution shift: a model validated in Boston may fail in Bamenda — or in the hospital across town. Population, equipment, and coding practices all shift performance.
  • Automation bias: humans over-trust confident machines. The corrective is procedural (verification steps), not attitudinal (telling yourself you’ll be careful).
  • Accountability: no AI carries a medical license. Every output that touches a patient or a chart is professionally yours after you accept it.
Course rule (Team21 Commandment 2, clinical edition): AI drafts, the clinician decides. Nothing generated in this course reaches a patient or a chart without your professional review — and Module 8 makes that rule institutional.
Reading companion: Eric Topol, Deep Medicine (the humanist case); WHO, Ethics and Governance of AI for Health (the governance frame — six principles from protecting human autonomy to ensuring inclusiveness and equity). Skim both this week; they anchor the capstone.

Going deeper — where clinical AI helps, and where it quietly harms

Evidence on clinical AI is uneven. The strongest current evidence of benefit is in administrative burden (documentation, inbox drafting, summarisation) and in specific, validated imaging tasks. Evidence that general chatbots improve patient outcomes in diagnosis is far weaker. A 2024 randomised study in JAMA Network Open found that giving physicians access to a large language model did not significantly improve their diagnostic reasoning scores, even though the model alone scored well — a reminder that human–AI teaming has to be designed, not assumed.

  • Automation bias: clinicians over-trust a confident system, especially under time pressure, and miss its errors. Countermeasure: form your own impression before reading the AI's.
  • Deskilling: over-reliance can erode skills. One multicentre study reported that endoscopists' adenoma detection fell when they returned to working without AI assistance. Keep deliberate unaided practice.
  • Equity drift: models trained on populations unlike yours can underperform for your patients — skin-tone differences in dermatology and pulse oximetry are well-documented examples of the broader problem.
The clinician's three questions for any AI output: What is this based on? How would I know if it's wrong? Who is accountable if I act on it? If you can't answer all three, the output is a prompt for thought, not a basis for action.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a clinical informatics lead. List the five most time-consuming non-patient-facing tasks in a typical week for a [specialty] clinician in [setting]. For each, rate the evidence that AI helps (strong / emerging / weak), the main safety risk, and one safeguard. Flag any task where AI should not be used.

📚 Glossary

  • Automation bias: Tendency to over-trust automated suggestions and overlook their errors
  • Deskilling: Loss of skill through reliance on automation
  • Human–AI teaming: How people and AI systems are combined in a workflow
  • Pajama time: After-hours documentation work

📖 References

  • Goh, E. et al. (2024). Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA Network Open.
  • Budzyń, K. et al. (2025). Endoscopist deskilling risk after exposure to AI in colonoscopy. Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology.

quiz.q: A hospital board in Douala reads that a frontier LLM passed a USMLE-style exam with a high score and proposes letting it answer ward nurses' dosing queries unsupervised. What is the most accurate response from the module?
opts: Exam performance matters little; the main barrier is that LLMs cannot read local formularies written in French
Exam results are irrelevant for LLMs because the questions were probably in training data, so the model has no real ability
Exam success is a real capability signal, not proof of safe practice; dosing answers still need verification
Exam performance proves clinical competence for knowledge tasks, so a short local pilot is enough before unsupervised use
quiz.x: Passing an exam is a capability signal, not practice; dosing is a foreground fact where hallucination risk demands verification. The runner-up (short pilot) still treats exam success as proof of competence.

quiz.q: A US health system's sepsis alert, bought from a large vendor, fires dozens of times per shift yet clinicians keep finding missed cases. Which lesson from the cautionary record best explains what should have happened before go-live?
opts: Clinicians should have received automation-bias training so they trust the alerts more consistently
External validation in the deploying population, measuring both missed cases and alert burden
The vendor should have published its training code so the hospital could reproduce the original accuracy
The alert threshold should have been lowered so that the model flags more patients and misses fewer
quiz.x: A widely used proprietary sepsis model missed many cases with heavy alert burden when externally validated; local validation is the lesson. Lowering the threshold worsens alert fatigue without addressing whether the model fits.

quiz.q: A commercial algorithm ranks patients for a care-management programme using predicted future healthcare spending. A Bamenda-trained analyst on the US team notices that sicker Black patients score lower. What is the root cause taught in the module?
opts: Clinicians entered fewer diagnoses for Black patients, a coding error the vendor can patch in the next release
The algorithm used race as an explicit input variable, which regulators should have prohibited at clearance
The model was trained on too few Black patients, so adding more training examples would fully correct it
Spending was used as a proxy for need, and unequal access to care means lower spending despite equal illness
quiz.x: The landmark analysis showed cost-as-proxy-for-need caused the bias: less access means less spending. More data or removing a race variable does not fix a biased target label.

quiz.q: A Cameroonian GP asks a general chatbot in October for the newest hypertension guideline thresholds; the guideline was revised two months earlier. Which limitation is MOST directly at play?
opts: Training cutoff and drift: the model lacks the recent change unless linked to live sources
Hallucination, because the model is inventing numbers that did not appear in any guideline
Automation bias, because the GP is likely to over-trust the confident answer it returns
Distribution shift, because the model was validated on patients from a different continent
quiz.x: The core issue is that the model does not know a change made after its training unless connected to live sources. Hallucination may co-occur, but the stem's defining feature is the recent revision.

quiz.q: A chest X-ray triage tool validated in a Boston academic centre is installed at a regional hospital in Bamenda with older portable machines and a high TB burden. Which concern deserves priority before relying on its flags?
opts: Training cutoff: the model will not know about this year's revisions to radiology reporting templates
Accountability: the vendor, not the radiologist, becomes liable for any missed finding at a new site
Hallucination: imaging models generate fabricated findings in the same way chatbots invent citations
Distribution shift: equipment, case mix and prevalence differ, so check performance locally
quiz.x: A model validated in Boston may fail in Bamenda because population, equipment and prevalence shift performance. Accountability matters, but it stays with clinicians and is not the first technical risk.

quiz.q: A department chair wants to reduce automation bias after residents copied an AI differential that missed an aortic dissection. Which countermeasure matches the module's advice?
opts: Build a procedural step: residents record their own differential before viewing the AI output
Restrict AI use to attendings, since experienced clinicians are not susceptible to automation bias
Remind residents in morning report to be sceptical and careful whenever they consult an AI tool
Switch to a newer model with a higher benchmark score so that fewer dangerous diagnoses are missed
quiz.x: The module says the corrective for automation bias is procedural (verification steps), not attitudinal. Reminders to 'be careful' are the attitudinal runner-up; attendings are also prone to it.

quiz.q: A clinic manager lists four tools: an ambient scribe, an FDA-cleared retinopathy screener, a no-show predictor and ChatGPT. Which pairing of tool and category follows the module's four-part taxonomy?
opts: Retinopathy screener = predictive/operational model, because it estimates the risk of future vision loss
No-show predictor = predictive/operational model, running inside the system and prone to bias and drift
ChatGPT = ambient documentation, because clinicians mainly use it to draft notes and referral letters
Ambient scribe = regulated diagnostic device, because it records clinical encounters for the medical record
quiz.x: No-show predictors are the classic operational model. The retinopathy screener is a regulated diagnostic device, a plausible confusion because it also involves risk.

quiz.q: A surgeon says: 'If the AI recommended it and it went wrong, the vendor carries the liability.' Using the module's five honest limits, what is the most defensible reply?
opts: Partly true: liability is split equally between the clinician and the vendor when an AI output is used
Correct for regulated devices, since FDA clearance transfers liability for algorithm errors to the manufacturer
The clinician who acts on the output remains accountable; AI cannot bear professional responsibility
Correct if the hospital signed a contract with an indemnity clause covering clinical decisions
quiz.x: Accountability stays with the clinician who acts. Contract indemnity (the runner-up) may shift some financial risk but not professional responsibility for the decision.

quiz.q: Eric Topol argues in Deep Medicine that AI's biggest gift could be restoring the human side of care. A Yaounde clinic director asks what this implies for deploying scribes. Which interpretation fits best?
opts: Delay deployment until AI is proven to outperform physicians, since the human side should stay untouched
Invest time saved in presence with patients, while keeping verification and oversight in place
Prefer AI that communicates empathetically with patients so clinicians can focus on technical decisions
Use the time saved to see more patients per hour, since access is the main human need in low-resource settings
quiz.x: Topol's point is returning time and presence to the clinician-patient bond; WHO adds the condition of ethics and oversight. Seeing more patients is a defensible use but contradicts the 'human side' argument.

quiz.q: Physicians in a US system log roughly two EHR hours per hour of direct care. The CMIO has budget for one AI pilot this year. Based on the evidence summary, which choice has the most robust value case today?
opts: Ambient documentation, where evaluations report less after-hours charting and lower burnout scores
An LLM chatbot answering patient portal messages directly without clinician review to clear the backlog
A proprietary sepsis early-warning score bought from the EHR vendor and activated across all wards
An autonomous differential-diagnosis engine for the emergency department to shorten time to disposition
quiz.x: The module calls documentation the most robust value case in clinical AI today. The sepsis model is the runner-up by appearance but has a documented poor external-validation record.

facts.t: Hours of EHR and desk work per hour of direct patient care in a landmark time-motion study.
facts.more: Sinsky et al. (2016) observed US ambulatory physicians spending nearly 2 hours on EHR and desk work for every hour with patients, plus after-hours 'pajama time'. Documentation is where clinical AI pays off first.
facts.src: Sinsky et al., Ann Intern Med 2016

facts.t: New citations indexed in PubMed every year.
facts.more: No clinician can keep up by reading alone. That is why retrieval and summarising tools matter, and why every AI summary must still be checked against the source.

facts.t: Why a widely used US risk algorithm under-referred Black patients.
facts.more: Obermeyer et al. (2019) showed the algorithm predicted healthcare cost as a proxy for need. Patients with less access to care spent less, so they looked healthier than they were. The bias lived in the proxy, not the maths.

facts.t: Ethical principles in WHO's guidance on AI for health.
facts.more: Protect autonomy; promote well-being, safety and the public interest; ensure transparency; foster accountability; ensure inclusiveness and equity; promote responsive, sustainable AI. They anchor the capstone governance note.

steps.s: A colleague shows an LLM's differential for a febrile child. It looks excellent and lists malaria third.
o: Adopt its ranking — the model passes licensing exams
Exam performance is not clinical validation, and it doesn't know your local prevalence.
Form your own impression first, then compare with the list
Right — your own assessment before reading the AI's counters automation bias.
Ignore it; LLMs have no place in diagnosis
Safe but wastes a useful 'what am I missing?' prompt. Use it after your own reasoning.

steps.s: Your director wants to buy a sepsis alert that scored very well at a large US hospital.
o: Ask for external validation and a local trial first
Correct — a widely deployed sepsis model missed many cases on external validation. Performance must be shown here.
Buy it; a big US system already trusts it
Distribution shift: population, equipment and coding differ. Validation does not travel automatically.
Buy it but tell staff to ignore it if it seems noisy
Unmonitored alert fatigue is how real cases get missed. Evaluate before deploying.

steps.s: After months with an AI polyp detector, the endoscopy team will lose it during a system upgrade.
o: No concern — skills don't fade in just a few months
A multicentre study reported lower adenoma detection after endoscopists returned to unaided work.
Cancel the upgrade so the AI is never offline for staff
Avoids the gap but ignores the risk. Downtime will happen eventually.
Plan unaided practice sessions and audit detection rates
Right — guard against deskilling with practice and measurement.

steps.s: An AI-drafted discharge summary you signed contained a wrong anticoagulant dose.
o: Report it, correct it, and add a dose check to your workflow
The signed output is yours. Fix the patient issue and the process.
Blame the software vendor clearly in the incident form
No AI carries a licence. Accepting the draft made it your professional act.
Stop using AI drafts for anything clinical from now on
Understandable, but a verification step keeps the time savings safely.

plaibox.win: Excellent — AI drafts, the clinician decides. You verified, validated locally and kept accountability.
plaibox.lose: Revisit the five limits: hallucination, drift, distribution shift, automation bias and accountability.

modules.d: Data discipline, the CLEAR framework at clinical grade, and the prompt patterns that survive contact with real practice.
modules.body:
Patient privacy before prompting — the non-negotiable layer

Under HIPAA (US) and equivalent regimes (GDPR in Europe, and national health-data laws elsewhere), Protected Health Information includes far more than names: dates of birth, medical record numbers, facial images, device identifiers, and — the trap most clinicians miss — combinations that re-identify, such as a rare diagnosis plus a small town plus an age. Consumer chatbots are not covered entities and offer no Business Associate Agreement (BAA); pasting PHI into them can constitute a reportable breach regardless of how helpful the output was.

  • Green path: institution-approved tools operating under a BAA or equivalent contract (many health systems now deploy HIPAA-eligible instances of major models), with data-retention and training-use terms in writing.
  • Amber path: consumer tools with rigorous de-identification — remove all 18 HIPAA identifier categories AND ask the re-identification question: could a motivated reader in my community identify this patient? If unsure, don’t.
  • Red path: raw clinical text, images with faces or identifiers, or protection-sensitive cases in any unapproved tool. Never.

De-identification in practice (do this, not just know it)

  • Swap specifics for clinical equivalents: "67-year-old man" not the name and DOB; "a regional referral hospital" not yours; "day 3 of admission" not the date.
  • Shift or bucket ages over 89, exact dates, and rare-disease geography.
  • Strip metadata from images; crop identifiers; never upload a face without explicit, documented consent and an approved tool.

CLEAR at clinical grade

The Team21 CLEAR framework (Persona · Tone · Format · Details · Target audience, plus Context, Reference, Iterate, Evaluate) becomes far more powerful when the Reference element carries clinical standards:

  • Persona: "You are a board-certified internist and medical educator who cites guidelines and flags uncertainty explicitly."
  • Format: name the artifact — SOAP note, SBAR handoff, ISBAR referral, discharge summary, AVS at 6th-grade reading level, table of differentials with discriminators.
  • Reference: "Guideline-concordant (name the guideline body relevant to you); distinguish what you know from what you infer; list every claim I must verify."
  • Evaluate: end prompts with "State your three largest uncertainties" — models are startlingly good at self-flagging when asked, and silent when not.

Seven prompt patterns that earn their place in your practice

  • The structured note: "Convert this de-identified encounter narrative into a SOAP note. Mark [INFERRED] anything not explicitly stated." The inference-marking instruction is the safety feature.
  • The dual-ranked differential: "Rank by likelihood AND separately by danger; for each, one discriminating question, one exam finding, one initial test." Dual ranking mirrors real clinical reasoning — common things commonly, deadly things always.
  • The devil’s-advocate consult: "My working diagnosis is X. Argue for the two most dangerous alternatives I might be anchoring away from." Anti-anchoring as a service.
  • The literacy transformer: "Rewrite these discharge instructions at 6th-grade level; keep all red-flag warnings verbatim in bold; then produce a French version." Health-literacy studies show most patient materials are written years above average reading level — this closes a real safety gap.
  • The guideline delta: "Summarize what changed between the prior and current guideline on [topic], as a table: recommendation, old, new, strength of evidence." (Then verify against the guideline itself — this pattern accelerates verification, never replaces it.)
  • The teach-back generator: "Write 5 teach-back questions to confirm this patient understood their new anticoagulant."
  • The attending simulator: "Act as a skeptical attending; pimp me on the physiology behind this presentation, one question at a time, escalating difficulty; correct me bluntly."

Verification discipline — the 60-second rule

For any clinical fact you did not already know: verify in a primary source before use. Doses and interactions against a formulary; claims against the guideline or a Module 4 evidence tool; citations by opening them (AI-fabricated references are the signature failure — assume fabricated until the DOI resolves). Sixty seconds of verification is the price of the hours AI saves you; clinicians who skip it eventually make the newspapers.

🧪 Interactive Lab — run this now

You are a board-certified clinician-educator. I will paste a DE-IDENTIFIED case. Produce: (1) a SOAP note marking every inference [INFERRED]; (2) a differential ranked by likelihood AND by danger with one discriminator each; (3) discharge instructions at 6th-grade reading level with red-flags in bold; (4) the same instructions in French; (5) a list titled VERIFY BEFORE USE containing every dose, claim, and citation I must confirm, with where to confirm each. Case: [paste de-identified case].

plAIbox™: run the lab on one real (de-identified) case from your week. Keep an error log: every correction you made to the AI output, categorized (factual / inferential / tone / omission). That log is a required capstone artifact — and the fastest calibration tool you will ever use.

Going deeper — de-identification that actually works

Under HIPAA's Safe Harbor method, 18 identifier types must be removed, including names, geographic units smaller than a state (with limited ZIP-code exceptions), all date elements except year (and ages over 89 must be aggregated), phone numbers, emails, record numbers, device identifiers, full-face photos and any other unique identifying characteristic. The alternative Expert Determination method uses a qualified expert to certify low re-identification risk. GDPR goes further: pseudonymised data (e.g. replacing names with codes) is still personal data.

  • Free text is the trap. "The only paediatric heart transplant in our district last March" identifies a child without a single name.
  • Images carry metadata. Photos and DICOM files can contain names and dates in headers or burned into pixels.
  • Approved tools change the rules. An institution-approved tool covered by a Business Associate Agreement (US) or a data processing agreement (EU) may be used with PHI within its approved scope; consumer chatbots generally are not.
Safe prompt pattern for consumer tools: "A [age-range] patient with [condition] on [drug class] presents with [symptoms]. What should be considered?" — no dates, no places, no rare-combination details. Then verify the answer against primary sources.

Clinical prompting that reduces hallucination

Ask for guideline citations with year, then check them; ask the model to state uncertainty and what would change its answer; and request differential considerations rather than single answers.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a privacy officer. Here is a clinical question I want to ask an AI tool: [paste, already stripped of names]. Identify any remaining identifiers or re-identifying combinations under HIPAA Safe Harbor and GDPR principles, rewrite it to be safely de-identified, and tell me what clinical meaning, if any, was lost.

📚 Glossary

  • PHI: Protected Health Information — identifiable health data under HIPAA
  • Safe Harbor: HIPAA de-identification by removing 18 identifier types
  • Expert Determination: HIPAA de-identification certified by a qualified expert
  • BAA: Business Associate Agreement — contract allowing a vendor to handle PHI
  • Pseudonymisation: Replacing identifiers with codes; still personal data under GDPR

📖 References

  • U.S. HHS — Guidance regarding methods for de-identification of PHI under the HIPAA Privacy Rule.
  • EU GDPR, Recital 26 and Article 4(5).

quiz.q: A Yaounde internist wants a consumer chatbot to help with a case: a 34-year-old with a rare lysosomal storage disease from a small village near Kumbo. She removes the name and record number. What is the best next judgement?
opts: Proceed, because removing name and record number satisfies de-identification for consumer tools
Stop and use the institutional tool, since rare diseases must not be discussed with any AI at all
Proceed but add 'please do not store this' to the prompt, which limits training on the content
Ask whether a local reader could re-identify her; rare disease plus village plus age likely could
quiz.x: The amber path requires removing identifiers AND asking the re-identification question; rare diagnosis plus small place plus age is the classic trap. Blanket refusal overstates the rule.

quiz.q: A US hospitalist pastes a full discharge summary into a free consumer chatbot because the output is excellent and 'nothing bad happened'. How does the module classify this?
opts: Acceptable, since harm is measured by outcome and no data has been leaked publicly so far
A minor policy lapse that becomes a breach once the patient later files a formal complaint
A possible reportable breach: consumer chatbots offer no BAA, however good the output was
Acceptable if the chatbot's privacy policy states that conversations are deleted within 30 days
quiz.x: Consumer chatbots are not covered entities and offer no BAA; pasting PHI can be a reportable breach regardless of output quality. A deletion policy is not a BAA.

quiz.q: A clinician needs to de-identify a case for an amber-path prompt: a 92-year-old woman admitted 14 March 2026 to Laquintinie Hospital. Which rewrite fits the module's technique?
opts: 'A woman over 90 admitted on day 0, now day 3 of admission, at a regional referral hospital'
'A 92-year-old woman admitted in March 2026 to a large hospital in Douala'
'Patient AB, aged 92, admitted 14/03 to Laquintinie', keeping her initials for tracking
'A very elderly woman admitted recently to a public hospital in Cameroon's economic capital'
quiz.x: Ages over 89 are bucketed, dates become relative days, and the hospital becomes generic. The first option still keeps an exact age over 89 and a month plus city that narrow identity.

quiz.q: A resident asks for a SOAP note from a de-identified narrative and wants protection against invented exam findings. Which instruction from the seven patterns is the built-in safety feature?
opts: 'Use the SOAP template exactly and keep the Assessment section under one hundred words'
'Write the plan in bullet points and list medications with doses at the bottom'
'Act as a board-certified internist who writes concise, guideline-concordant notes'
'Mark as [INFERRED] anything not explicitly stated in the narrative I gave you'
quiz.x: The structured-note pattern's safety feature is inference-marking. The persona instruction improves tone and accuracy but does not flag fabricated content.

quiz.q: A Bamenda emergency physician asks an AI for a differential for acute chest pain in a 45-year-old. Which prompt best mirrors 'common things commonly, deadly things always'?
opts: 'Argue for the most dangerous diagnosis first and explain why the common causes are less important here'
'List the ten most likely causes in order, with the estimated prevalence of each in sub-Saharan African adults'
'Rank by likelihood and separately by danger; give a discriminating question, exam finding and test for each'
'Give the single most likely diagnosis with confidence level, then the investigations needed to confirm it'
quiz.x: Dual ranking by likelihood and danger is the module's pattern. The devil's-advocate option is useful against anchoring but downplays common causes rather than ranking both.

quiz.q: A clinician uses AI to rewrite warfarin discharge instructions for a patient with limited literacy and needs a French copy too. Which prompt detail is most important to preserve safety?
opts: Ask for the shortest possible version so the patient is not overwhelmed by text on discharge
Ask for a 6th-grade level with red-flag warnings kept verbatim in bold, then a French version
Ask for the French version first, since translation errors matter more than reading level
Ask for a friendly tone with emojis to improve engagement, then verify the warfarin dose manually
quiz.x: The literacy transformer keeps red-flag warnings verbatim while lowering reading level. Shortest-possible is the runner-up but risks dropping the warnings.

quiz.q: A chatbot gives a GP an elegant summary with five journal references on a new SGLT2 indication. Under the 60-second rule, what should she assume about the references?
opts: Assume fabricated until each DOI resolves and the paper is opened to confirm the claim
They are reliable if the journal names and years look plausible and match known publishers
They are reliable if the chatbot states it is confident and lists a DOI for each reference
They are probably real but may be misquoted, so reading the abstracts in the chat is enough
quiz.x: Fabricated references are the signature failure; assume fabricated until the DOI resolves. Even a listed DOI can be invented, which is why the runner-up falls short.

quiz.q: A nephrologist ends prompts with 'State your three largest uncertainties.' A colleague calls this a waste of tokens. Which justification from the CLEAR Evaluate element is strongest?
opts: It lets the clinician skip verification on the claims that the model did not flag as uncertain
Models self-flag uncertainty well when asked and stay silent when not, guiding what to verify
It makes the answer longer, which tends to correlate with higher accuracy on clinical questions
It forces the model to cite guidelines, which reduces hallucination to a negligible level
quiz.x: Models are good at self-flagging when asked and silent when not; the flags direct verification. Skipping checks on unflagged claims is the dangerous misreading.

quiz.q: A dermatologist in Texas wants AI input on a facial lesion photo from a patient who verbally agreed in clinic. The only available tool is a consumer chatbot. What does the module require?
opts: Upload after blurring the eyes, which removes the full-face identifier among HIPAA's 18 categories
Upload it, because verbal consent in clinic covers sharing the image with any AI assistant
Do not upload: facial images need explicit documented consent and an approved tool, which is absent here
Upload, since images are not PHI unless they are attached to a name or medical record number
quiz.x: Faces require explicit documented consent plus an approved tool; both must be met. Blurring eyes is a partial fix that still leaves an identifiable full-face image.

quiz.q: A cardiologist asks an AI to summarise changes between the 2021 and 2025 versions of a heart-failure guideline as a table. How should she use the output?
opts: Use it if a second chatbot independently produces the same table with matching rows

modules.t: Tool Study I: Documentation & Ambient Scribes
modules.d: The market mapped, the economics computed, and the pilot playbook for getting one.
modules.body:
Why scribes are the beachhead

Documentation is where clinical AI pays for itself first because the task is bounded (one visit → one note), the ground truth is nearby (you were in the room), and the value is immediate (your evening back). Health systems deploying ambient scribes at scale report the largest burnout-score improvements of any recent intervention. Master this category and you will understand how to evaluate every other one.

How ambient scribes actually work

  • Capture: with explicit patient consent, the visit audio is recorded (phone or room mic). Consent scripts and jurisdictional recording laws are part of deployment, not afterthoughts.
  • ASR + diarization: speech-to-text with speaker separation — robust to accents and interruptions in modern systems, still challenged by heavy crosstalk and some code-switching.
  • Generation: an LLM transforms transcript to note in your template (SOAP, APSO, specialty formats), often with orders, problem lists, and patient instructions drafted alongside.
  • Review & sign: you edit and sign. Editing time is the honest metric — a scribe that saves dictation but demands heavy correction saves nothing.

The market, mapped by how you buy

  • Enterprise (bought by health systems): Microsoft DAX Copilot (Nuance) — the incumbent heavyweight, deep Epic integration, procured institutionally; Abridge — enterprise-grade with strong published evidence and major system partnerships, similarly institution-level. If you are employed by a large system, these arrive via your CMIO, not your credit card.
  • Self-serve (bought by clinicians): Heidi Health — free tier plus paid plans, minutes-to-start, popular with GPs, students, and clinics worldwide including low-resource settings; Freed — subscription (~$99/month class), built for independent clinicians, minimal IT; Suki — solo and group licensing with real EHR integrations (Epic, Cerner, athena), the mid-market bridge.
  • Watch the churn: this market moves quarterly — pricing, tiers, and EHR integrations in this module are teaching snapshots. Your capstone matrix requires you to verify current terms, which is itself the skill.

The selection matrix (your capstone artifact)

  • Integration: writes into your EHR vs copy-paste (copy-paste is fine solo, fails at clinic scale).
  • Consent & legality: recording-consent workflow matched to your jurisdiction (one-party vs all-party consent states/countries differ).
  • Template quality in YOUR specialty: a scribe brilliant in primary care may fumble psychiatry’s nuance or ophthalmology’s notation — trial with your own visit types.
  • Contract: BAA/DPA, data retention, training-use opt-out, breach terms — in writing.
  • Economics: price per clinician per month ÷ minutes saved per day. At even 30 minutes/day saved, a $99/month tool costs roughly $0.16 per saved minute — the cheapest clinician time ever purchased. Compute your own number honestly, including editing time.
  • Edge behavior: accents, interpreter visits, telehealth audio, offline/low-bandwidth conduct.

The pilot playbook (how individuals move institutions)

  • Week 0: pick 2 self-serve tools; get IT/privacy sign-off for a de-identified or consented trial per policy.
  • Weeks 1–2: 10 visits per tool. Log: minutes to complete note before vs after, edits per note, patient reactions to consent.
  • Week 3: one-page memo to your medical director — time data, quality samples, consent workflow, cost per clinician, and the ask (a funded 5-clinician pilot). Template provided in course resources. This memo has launched more institutional deployments than any vendor demo.
🧪 Interactive Lab

Act as a health-IT procurement analyst. Build me a scribe selection matrix as a table: rows = [tools I am considering]; columns = EHR integration, consent workflow fit for [my jurisdiction], specialty template quality for [my specialty], contract protections (BAA/DPA, training opt-out), monthly cost, estimated minutes saved per day, cost per saved minute, and open risks. Then draft the one-page pilot memo to my medical director using placeholder data I will replace.

Going deeper — evaluating a scribe like a clinician-scientist

Before a department adopts an ambient scribe, run a structured local evaluation rather than relying on vendor demos.

  • Error taxonomy: classify every correction as omission (missed a relevant finding), fabrication (documented something that wasn't said or done — e.g. an examination never performed), misattribution (the patient's words recorded as the clinician's), or style. Fabrications and omissions are the safety-critical ones.
  • Edit burden: measure time from visit end to note signed, and minutes of editing per note, before and after.
  • Subgroups: test with accents, languages, interpreters, multiple speakers and noisy rooms. Performance often drops in exactly the encounters where documentation matters most.
  • Consent and transparency: tell patients the visit is being recorded for documentation, offer an opt-out, and follow local law on recording consent.
Signature means ownership. When you sign an AI-drafted note, it is your note. A fabricated "normal cardiovascular exam" you didn't perform is a medico-legal and patient-safety problem, not a software bug.

What early evidence shows

Published evaluations and large health-system rollouts report reductions in documentation time and burnout scores for many users, with wide individual variation; time savings per note are often modest, and the benefit is frequently felt as reduced cognitive load. Treat vendor claims as hypotheses to test locally.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a clinical quality lead. Design a four-week local evaluation of an ambient scribe for [specialty]: sample size, measures (time to sign, edit minutes, error taxonomy counts), subgroups to test, patient consent wording, and a go/no-go rule. Include a one-page error log template.

📚 Glossary

  • Ambient scribe: AI that listens to a visit and drafts the clinical note
  • Fabrication: Documenting something that didn't occur
  • Omission: Leaving out a clinically relevant finding
  • Edit burden: Time spent correcting AI drafts

📖 References

  • Tierney, A.A. et al. (2024). Ambient artificial intelligence scribes to alleviate the burden of clinical documentation. NEJM Catalyst.

modules.t: Tool Study II: Knowledge & Decision Support
modules.d: Matching the tool to the question: point-of-care evidence, differentials, and the research engine stack.
modules.body:
The taxonomy of clinical questions

Clinicians ask four distinguishable kinds of questions, and the tool that excels at one fails at another. Mislabeling the question is the root of most disappointment with clinical AI:

  • Background ("What is X?"): settled knowledge — mechanisms, classifications, definitions. General LLMs excel; risk is low because errors are checkable against any textbook.
  • Foreground ("In this patient, should I…?"): evidence-dependent decisions. This is where citation-grounded tools earn their existence.
  • Reasoning support ("What am I missing?"): differential expansion, anti-anchoring. LLMs are strong brainstorm partners here precisely because breadth beats precision at this step.
  • Synthesis ("What does the literature say?"): research-grade questions needing systematic retrieval — the Module 5 stack.

The point-of-care evidence tier

  • OpenEvidence: free for verified clinicians (registration/NPI-class verification); answers foreground questions with citations drawn from the literature; has spread through US residency programs at remarkable speed precisely because it closes the citation gap that makes bare LLMs unsafe for foreground use.
  • UpToDate (with arriving AI features): the editorial gold standard — humans synthesize, grade, and take responsibility; institutional or personal subscription. When stakes are high and time is short, curated beats generated.
  • Glass Health: AI-assisted differentials and plan drafting built for clinicians; subscription with trial; particularly strong as a teaching scaffold — compare its differential to yours and interrogate the gaps.
  • General LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini): unbeatable for background explanation, drafting, transformation, and reasoning support; for foreground facts, treat every claim as unverified until checked against the tier above. The same model that beautifully explains renal physiology will occasionally invent a dosing threshold with identical confidence.

The research engine stack (preview of Module 5)

  • Elicit: screen and extract from papers at scale — inclusion screening, structured data extraction into tables; free tier + paid.
  • Consensus: "what does the literature say about X" with citation-backed synthesis and study-level claims.
  • Scite: the killer feature — shows whether citing papers support or contrast a claim, turning citation counts into citation directions.
  • Semantic Scholar + PubMed: the free foundations under every stack; modern PubMed plus an LLM for query-building is still the workhorse of serious searching.

Failure modes by tool class (know these cold)

  • Bare LLMs on foreground questions: fabricated specifics — the classic. Mitigation: citation-grounded tools or verify-every-claim discipline.
  • Citation-grounded tools: real citations, sometimes shallow reading of them — the paper exists but says less than implied. Mitigation: open the key citation for consequential decisions.
  • Curated references: lag on brand-new evidence and cost money. Mitigation: pair with alert services for your specialty.
  • All tools: your question framing dominates output quality — garbage question, confident garbage answer. The four-type taxonomy IS the prompt-engineering.
🧪 Interactive Lab — the four-way bake-off

I am comparing clinical knowledge tools. Here is one real foreground question from my practice this week: [state it precisely, PICO-style if possible]. First, classify my question (background / foreground / reasoning / synthesis) and critique its framing. Then answer it as well as you can, explicitly separating: (a) what you are confident of, (b) what you infer, (c) exactly which claims I must verify and the best primary source for each. I will run this same question through a citation-grounded tool and compare.

plAIbox™ (graded): run one real foreground question through four routes — a general LLM, OpenEvidence (or equivalent), UpToDate if you have access, and manual PubMed. Build a one-page comparison: speed, citation quality, accuracy, and precisely where each route would have misled you. Present to your cohort; the collective error map is the real curriculum.

Going deeper — appraising AI answers with evidence-based medicine

Clinical decision support tools that cite literature (e.g. OpenEvidence, or the AI features increasingly built into established point-of-care references) are more useful for foreground questions than general chatbots — but citations are a starting point for appraisal, not the end of it.

  • Check the level of evidence: is the cited source a systematic review or RCT, a cohort study, or expert opinion? An answer supported only by a case series is weak.
  • Check applicability: does the study population match your patient — age, comorbidities, setting, region? Many trials exclude older adults, pregnant patients and people with multiple conditions.
  • Check currency: guidelines change. Confirm the version and year, and look for updates.
  • Check the claim matches the source: open the abstract. Models sometimes cite a real paper that doesn't support the stated claim.
Drug questions: doses, interactions and renal or hepatic adjustments should be confirmed in an authoritative drug reference or with a pharmacist, never taken from a general chatbot alone.

Using AI for differential diagnosis safely

AI can be useful for broadening a differential ("what am I missing?"), especially for rare conditions. Use it after your own assessment, treat its list as prompts for further history and investigation, and watch for confident, specific suggestions that pull you away from common causes.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are an evidence-based medicine tutor. Here is an AI answer to a clinical question, with its citations: [paste]. For each citation, tell me what I need to check: study design and level of evidence, population and applicability to my patient, publication year and whether guidelines have changed, and whether the source actually supports the claim.

📚 Glossary

  • Foreground question: A patient-specific question about management or diagnosis
  • Level of evidence: Ranking of study designs by reliability
  • Applicability: Whether study findings fit a specific patient or setting
  • Point-of-care reference: A curated, regularly updated clinical knowledge resource

📖 References

  • Guyatt, G. et al. Users' Guides to the Medical Literature. JAMA/McGraw-Hill.
  • Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine — Levels of Evidence.

quiz.q: A resident asks: 'In this 70-year-old with CKD stage 4 and new atrial fibrillation, should I start apixaban, and at what dose?' How should this question be classified and routed?

Synthesis question, requiring a systematic literature search with Elicit before deciding on therapy
Reasoning-support question, best answered by asking an LLM to expand the differential
Background question, so a general LLM explanation is adequate and low risk

quiz.q: A medical student wants to understand the mechanism of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system before an exam. Which tool choice fits the four-type taxonomy best?

A general LLM, since background questions are low risk and errors are checkable in any textbook

OpenEvidence, since citation-grounded answers are required for any medical fact

Run a Consensus query on the diagnostic accuracy of chest X-ray in elderly patients

quiz.x: Reasoning support (what am I missing?) is where LLMs are strong brainstorm partners because breadth beats precision. Checking criteria in UpToDate reinforces the anchor rather than challenging it.

quiz.q: A cardiologist sees that a key paper is cited 400 times and assumes the claim is settled. Which tool feature addresses her error most directly?

Semantic Scholar's ranking of the most influential citing papers by field
OpenEvidence's summarised answer with citations drawn from recent literature
Elicit's structured extraction of populations and outcomes into a comparison table
quiz.x: Scite turns citation counts into citation directions. Influence rankings still count citations without showing whether they agree.

quiz.q: OpenEvidence gives a well-referenced answer recommending a drug in pregnancy; the referenced paper is real. Which failure mode should the clinician still check for before acting?
opts: Training cutoff, since citation-grounded tools cannot index papers from the last two years
Shallow reading: the paper exists but may say less than the answer implies, so open it
Fabricated citations, the classic failure of citation-grounded tools on foreground questions
Distribution shift, since the tool was validated mostly on US residency program questions
quiz.x: The module's failure mode for citation-grounded tools is real citations read shallowly. Fabrication is the bare-LLM failure, the near-miss distractor.

quiz.q: At 2 a.m. a Douala emergency physician must manage a potassium of 7.4 mmol/L quickly. He has UpToDate, a general LLM and Consensus. Which follows the module's rule for this situation?
opts: Ask two general LLMs and act if their recommendations agree on the main steps
Use Consensus to see what the literature says before acting on any local hyperkalaemia protocol
Use UpToDate, because curated beats generated when stakes are high and time is short
Use the general LLM, as its speed matters most when the decision is urgent
quiz.x: When stakes are high and time is short, curated beats generated. Two agreeing LLMs is the runner-up but can share the same fabricated specifics.

quiz.q: A program director notices residents getting confident nonsense from AI. Their prompts read: 'tell me about diabetes treatment'. What does the module identify as the main fix?
opts: Use citation-grounded tools exclusively, which correct vague questions automatically
Frame the question precisely (PICO-style where possible), because framing dominates output
Add a persona instruction asking the model to act as an endocrinologist
Upgrade to a more capable model, since output quality mainly depends on model size
quiz.x: Question framing dominates output quality; the four-type taxonomy is the prompt engineering. A persona helps a little but does not fix an unanswerable vague question.

quiz.q: UpToDate is the editorial gold standard, yet a new landmark trial was published last week. What mitigation does the module pair with curated references?
opts: Rely on UpToDate anyway, because editors review all trials before they affect practice
Replace UpToDate with a general LLM, which tends to incorporate newly published trials more quickly
Pair the curated reference with alert services for your specialty to catch brand-new evidence
Search Consensus weekly and override UpToDate whenever a newer trial appears there
quiz.x: Curated references lag and cost money; pair them with specialty alert services. Overriding curation whenever a single new trial appears skips appraisal.

quiz.q: An AI tool cites a single retrospective cohort to support a change in practice. Using evidence-based appraisal from the module, what should the clinician weigh first?
opts: Whether the AI tool expressed high confidence in its recommendation
Whether the cohort was published in a high-impact journal within the last year or two
Whether the study sample size was above one thousand patients
The level of evidence: one observational study ranks below RCTs and systematic reviews
quiz.x: Citations are a starting point for appraisal; level of evidence comes first. Sample size matters but a large observational study is still prone to confounding.

quiz.q: A Glass Health differential differs from a student's own list for a febrile child returning from Garoua. How does the module suggest using this tool for learning?
opts: Use it as a scaffold: compare its differential with hers and interrogate the gaps
Set it aside until she qualifies, since students should not use clinical decision tools
Use it just for adult patients, since paediatric differentials are outside its scope
Replace her list with Glass Health's, since it is built specifically for clinicians
quiz.x: Glass Health is strong as a teaching scaffold; compare and interrogate gaps. Replacing her own list removes the learning and invites automation bias.

facts.t: Background, foreground, reasoning support and synthesis questions.
facts.more: Mislabelling the question is the root of most disappointment with clinical AI. Each type has a best tool — and a tool that will mislead.

facts.t: Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome — the frame for a foreground question.
facts.more: A precise PICO question gets better answers from every tool, from PubMed to citation-grounded AI.

modules.t: AI for Medical Research & Academic Writing
modules.d: From question to published paper: the accelerated pipeline, the statistics guardrails, and the integrity rules journals now enforce.
modules.body:
The research pipeline, accelerated stage by stage

  • 1. Question formulation: "Convert my vague interest — [topic] — into three answerable questions in PICO format (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome); for each, state the study design that could answer it and the datasets or populations that would be required." Ten minutes of this dialogue routinely saves a month of drift.
  • 2. Search strategy: LLMs draft Boolean strings with MeSH terms for PubMed/Embase ("draft, then librarian-verify" is the professional standard — medical librarians report AI-drafted strings are strong starting points and poor final ones).
  • 3. Screening: Elicit and systematic-review platforms with AI assistance triage titles/abstracts against your inclusion criteria. Governance rule from the Cochrane world: AI may assist screening, but human adjudication of borderline calls — and documentation of the AI’s role — is required for a defensible methods section.
  • 4. Extraction: structured tables (population, n, intervention, outcomes, effect sizes, risk-of-bias notes) generated per paper, then spot-audited: verify a random 20% by hand and report your audit in methods. Auditable acceleration is publishable; unaudited acceleration is not.
  • 5. Synthesis: ask for contradictions, not just summaries: "Where do these studies disagree, and what design differences could explain it?" — the question that turns a literature pile into a discussion section.
  • 6. Writing: outline → section drafts → your intellectual pass (the argument must be yours) → AI polish pass for clarity and concision → reference verification, one by one, by opening them. The fabricated-citation retractions now on record all share one feature: nobody opened the references.

Statistics: the guardrails

  • Legitimate: "Which test fits this design and why? What assumptions must I check? Interpret this output in plain language. What would invalidate this conclusion?" AI as statistics tutor and interpretation checker is transformative for clinician-researchers.
  • Illegitimate: letting AI choose and run analyses you don’t understand, or generate results you can’t defend at a podium. The test: if a reviewer asks "why this test?", the answer must be yours.
  • The p-hacking amplifier: AI makes running twenty analyses trivially easy — which makes pre-registration and stated primary outcomes MORE important, not less. Speed without discipline manufactures false findings faster.

Integrity: what journals and institutions now require

  • Authorship: ICMJE-aligned journals prohibit listing AI as an author — authorship requires accountability, which machines cannot bear.
  • Disclosure: most major journals require describing AI use in methods or acknowledgments (which tool, for what tasks). Norms vary — check the specific journal, every submission.
  • Peer review: many funders and journals prohibit feeding confidential manuscripts into AI tools for review purposes — confidentiality of submission survives the AI era intact.
  • Data: research data carries its own consent and governance terms; "de-identified for care" is not automatically "approved for AI processing" — check your protocol and IRB/ethics terms.
🧪 Interactive Lab

Act as a methodologist and co-investigator. My research interest: [describe loosely]. (1) Refine it into three PICO-format questions ranked by feasibility for a clinician with limited time and no funding. (2) For the best one: draft a PubMed Boolean search string with MeSH terms, an inclusion/exclusion table, and a data-extraction template. (3) List the statistical approach with its assumptions, and every point where I must involve a librarian, statistician, or ethics committee. (4) Draft my AI-use disclosure statement for a journal.

plAIbox™ (graded): the mini-review. One focused question, ten papers, AI-assisted screening and extraction with a documented 20% hand-audit, a 500-word synthesis whose every citation you opened, and a methods-style AI-disclosure paragraph. Two weeks; mentor plays peer reviewer. Past students have expanded this artifact into published letters and posters.

Going deeper — research integrity in the AI era

Journals and publishers now have explicit AI policies. Most follow the position of the ICMJE and COPE: AI tools cannot be listed as authors, because they cannot take responsibility for the work, and authors must disclose AI use, typically in the methods or acknowledgements. Check each journal's current policy before submission.

  • Fabricated references: LLMs can produce plausible but non-existent citations. Every reference must be located and read. Reference managers that verify DOIs help.
  • Data analysis: if AI writes your statistical code, you must understand and check it. Ask it to explain each step, run checks on a sample, and confirm assumptions (normality, independence, missing data handling).
  • Systematic reviews: AI can help screen titles and abstracts, but report its role transparently (PRISMA 2020 asks for details of automation tools) and use dual human screening or validation on a sample.
  • Peer review confidentiality: uploading a manuscript you're reviewing to a public AI tool may breach confidentiality; many publishers and funders, including the NIH for grant review, prohibit it.
Disclosure template: "During preparation of this work the authors used [tool] to [purpose, e.g. improve language clarity]. After using this tool, the authors reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the content of the publication."
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a research integrity adviser. Here is my study plan and how I intend to use AI at each stage: [paste]. Flag any use that conflicts with ICMJE/COPE guidance or confidentiality rules, suggest how to validate AI-assisted screening or analysis, and draft a disclosure statement for my manuscript.

📚 Glossary

  • ICMJE: International Committee of Medical Journal Editors
  • COPE: Committee on Publication Ethics
  • PRISMA 2020: Reporting guideline for systematic reviews
  • PICO: Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome

📖 References

  • ICMJE (2024). Recommendations — Artificial Intelligence (AI)-Assisted Technology.
  • COPE Position Statement: Authorship and AI tools (2023).
  • Page, M.J. et al. (2021). The PRISMA 2020 statement. BMJ.
  • NIH Notice NOT-OD-23-149 on use of generative AI in peer review.

quiz.q: A Yaounde paediatrician has a vague interest in 'malaria and anaemia in children'. Which first AI step from the pipeline would save the most wasted effort?

Ask AI to draft the introduction and discussion so the argument is clear from the outset
Ask AI to choose the statistical test that best fits a study of anaemia outcomes
Ask Elicit to screen all papers on malaria and anaemia published in the last ten years

quiz.q: A team used Elicit to screen 1,200 abstracts. For a defensible methods section under Cochrane-style governance, what is still required?

Human adjudication of borderline calls and documentation of the AI's role in screening
Nothing further, provided the tool's sensitivity has been published by the vendor
Re-screening all 1,200 abstracts manually so that every single AI decision is confirmed by a human
quiz.x: AI may assist screening, but humans adjudicate borderline calls and the AI role is documented. Re-screening everything is defensible but forfeits the benefit.

5 papers (10%), reported in the supplementary material
10 papers (20%), reported in the methods section
All 50 papers, reported in the acknowledgements
quiz.x: The module says verify a random 20% by hand and report the audit in methods: 20% of 50 is 10. Auditable acceleration is publishable.

quiz.q: A US resident submits a manuscript listing 'ChatGPT (OpenAI)' as fourth author for drafting help. How will an ICMJE-aligned journal likely respond?

Accept it, because listing AI as author is the most transparent form of disclosure
Reject the manuscript outright, since any AI drafting breaches ICMJE authorship policies
Decline the authorship: AI cannot be accountable; disclose its use in methods or acknowledgments
quiz.x: Authorship requires accountability, which machines cannot bear; use is disclosed instead. Rejecting all AI-assisted manuscripts overstates current policy.

quiz.q: A reviewer receives a confidential manuscript and wants an AI to summarise its weaknesses. What do many journals and funders require?

It is allowed if the reviewer discloses the AI use in the confidential comments to the editor
It is encouraged, since AI reduces reviewer fatigue and improves consistency
Many prohibit feeding confidential manuscripts into AI tools for review
quiz.x: Confidentiality of submission survives the AI era; many funders and journals prohibit this. A no-training paid tier is the runner-up but still breaks confidentiality policies.

quiz.q: Using AI, a fellow ran 20 different analyses of a registry and found one with p = 0.03. What does the module say is the right response?
opts: Report it, adding a transparent note in the methods that AI was used to run the analyses
Re-run the same analysis in a second AI tool to confirm the p-value
Treat it as likely chance; pre-registration and a stated primary outcome matter more with AI
Report the significant analysis, since AI chose it objectively from all possible tests
quiz.x: With 20 tests at alpha 0.05, about one false positive is expected; AI amplifies p-hacking. Reconfirming the same p-value elsewhere checks arithmetic, not chance.

quiz.q: A clinician-researcher asks AI: 'Which test fits my design, what assumptions must I check, and what would invalidate my conclusion?' How does the module rate this use?
opts: Illegitimate: statistical choices must be made by a statistician before AI is involved at all
Legitimate: AI as statistics tutor and interpretation checker, with the reasoning remaining hers
Illegitimate: AI explanations of assumptions are often fabricated and cannot be relied on
Legitimate provided the AI also runs the analysis so the outputs are consistent
quiz.x: Tutor and interpretation-checker use is legitimate, provided the answer to 'why this test?' is hers. Letting AI also run analyses she does not understand crosses the line.

quiz.q: A registry in Bamenda holds de-identified data collected for clinical care. A doctor wants to process it with an AI tool for a research paper. What must she check first?

Whether the AI tool's servers are located inside Cameroon
Whether the target journal accepts AI-assisted analyses for registry-based observational studies
Nothing, because de-identified data falls outside data-protection laws
quiz.x: 'De-identified for care' is not automatically 'approved for AI processing'; check protocol and ethics terms. Server location may matter legally but is secondary.

quiz.q: Several recent retractions involved fabricated references in AI-assisted papers. What single practice does the module say all those cases lacked?
opts: Using a citation manager to format references in the journal's style
Opening and checking each reference one by one before submission
Running the manuscript through an AI-detection tool before submission
Asking the AI to state its confidence in every reference it provided
quiz.x: The retractions all share one feature: nobody opened the references. A citation manager formats fabricated references just as neatly.

quiz.q: A team asks AI for a synthesis of 12 trials on a tuberculosis regimen. Which prompt best turns the literature into a discussion section?
opts: 'Where do these studies disagree, and what design differences could explain it?'
'Write a balanced conclusion recommending the regimen if most trials favour it'
'List the trials with the largest sample sizes and summarise their main findings'
'Summarise each of these 12 trials in one paragraph, in chronological order'
quiz.x: Asking for contradictions and design explanations turns a pile into a discussion. Summaries by size or date are useful but just reorder the pile.

facts.t: ICMJE-aligned journals do not allow AI tools to be listed as authors.
facts.more: Authorship requires accountability for the work, which a machine cannot bear. AI use must instead be disclosed, usually in methods or acknowledgements.

facts.t: The PRISMA 2020 checklist for reporting systematic reviews.
facts.more: PRISMA 2020 asks authors to report automation tools used in the review process — including AI-assisted screening.

facts.t: The course's hand-audit rule for AI-extracted data.
facts.more: Verify a random fifth of AI extractions by hand and report the audit in methods. Auditable acceleration is publishable; unaudited acceleration is not.

facts.more: Uploading confidential applications or manuscripts to AI tools breaches confidentiality. Many journals apply similar rules.

modules.t: AI for Medical Students: Study Systems
modules.d: Boards, wards, and OSCEs: building the study machine that compounds — with the science of why it works.
modules.body:
The learning science first — why these systems work

Two findings dominate a century of learning research: active recall (testing yourself beats re-reading by large margins) and spaced repetition (reviews timed just before forgetting lock in retention). Medical students discovered this at scale — spaced-repetition flashcards became boards-prep orthodoxy — but making good cards and good practice questions was always the bottleneck. AI removes the bottleneck. What follows is the study machine, component by component.

Component 1: The card factory (active recall at scale)

  • "From these lecture notes, generate cloze-deletion flashcards: one fact per card, no card answerable without the concept, include a one-line ‘why it matters clinically’ on the back. Output in a format I can import to Anki."
  • Quality control is yours: delete cards testing trivia, keep cards testing decisions. A 40-card deck you curated beats a 400-card dump.

Component 2: The question generator (boards-grade practice)

  • "Write 5 USMLE-style clinical vignettes on [topic]: two-step reasoning (finding → mechanism → answer), plausible distractors representing real student errors, and explanations for why EVERY option is right or wrong."
  • The explanation-for-every-option requirement is the pedagogy: wrong-answer autopsy is where discrimination skill is built.
  • Calibration warning: AI-generated questions are excellent practice and imperfect calibrators — difficulty drifts from real exams. Use question banks for calibration; use AI for volume, weak-spot targeting, and explanation depth.

Component 3: The standardized patient (voice mode changes everything)

  • "You are a standardized patient: 54-year-old with an undisclosed diagnosis (choose one appropriate to chest pain teaching). Present realistically; volunteer nothing; reveal only what I elicit. After 8 minutes, break character and score my history-taking: organization, red-flag coverage, empathy, and the three questions I failed to ask."
  • Run it by voice. Students consistently report the first session is startling — the hesitation, the missed questions, the timing all feel real. Repeat weekly with rotating chief complaints.

Component 4: OSCE & communication rehearsal

  • Counseling stations: smoking cessation, new-diagnosis diabetes, inhaler technique — request a rubric-scored debrief after each.
  • Breaking bad news with SPIKES (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy): "Play the patient’s spouse; I will deliver difficult news; score my SPIKES adherence step by step and quote the exact sentences that landed well or poorly." Rehearsing the hardest conversations in a consequence-free room is a gift no previous generation of students had.

Component 5: The concept rescuer

  • The three-level ladder: "Explain [renal tubular acidosis] to a 12-year-old, then to a nursing student, then to an attending — same core truth, three altitudes." When you can follow all three, you own the concept.
  • The Feynman inversion: "I will explain [concept] to YOU; interrupt at every gap or error." Teaching the machine exposes what re-reading conceals.

The integrity line for students

  • AI on graded work follows your school’s policy, full stop — and disclosure norms from Module 5 apply to student research identically.
  • The deeper point: shortcuts on formation become gaps at the bedside. Use AI to practice MORE, never to practice less. The machine is your sparring partner, not your substitute.
🧪 Interactive Lab — your first simulated patient

You are a standardized patient for a medical student. Choose an undisclosed diagnosis appropriate for teaching [chief complaint of my choice]. Present realistically with a natural personality; volunteer nothing; reveal findings only when properly elicited. After 8 minutes (or when I say STOP), break character and give me: a score out of 10 for organization, red-flag coverage, and empathy; the three most important questions I failed to ask; and the diagnosis with the discriminating features I found or missed.

plAIbox™ (graded): build and run your study OS for one full week — card factory, question generator, one voice-mode patient, one OSCE rehearsal — and report: hours spent vs your previous baseline, question-bank score movement, and the single component you will keep forever. Mentors review the system design, not just the report.

Going deeper — using AI to learn, not to avoid learning

The risk for students is fluency illusion: reading a clear AI explanation feels like understanding, but recognition isn't recall. The learning science is clear that effortful retrieval, spacing, interleaving and explaining in your own words produce durable learning.

  • Generate, then check: answer the question or draw the pathway yourself first, then ask AI to critique. Reversing this order produces the illusion.
  • Quality-control AI cards and questions: AI-generated flashcards and MCQs can contain subtle errors. Check them against your textbook or lecture notes, especially numbers and drug facts. One wrong card reviewed 30 times becomes a wrong memory.
  • Interleave: mix topics in practice sessions (cardiology, renal, pharmacology) rather than blocking one topic; it feels harder but improves discrimination between similar presentations.
  • Simulated patients: AI role-play is useful for history taking and communication practice. Ask it to play a patient with a hidden diagnosis and to reveal information only when you ask the right question, then give feedback.
Integrity: follow your school's policy on AI in assessed work. Using AI to study is generally encouraged; submitting AI-written work as your own usually is not.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a simulated patient for a medical student. Choose a hidden diagnosis appropriate for a [year] student in [specialty]. Answer only what I ask, as a real patient would, without medical jargon. When I say 'end', reveal the diagnosis, score my history taking against a checklist, and list the three most important questions I missed.

📚 Glossary

  • Active recall: Retrieving information from memory to strengthen it
  • Spaced repetition: Reviewing at increasing intervals before forgetting
  • Interleaving: Mixing different topics within practice sessions
  • Fluency illusion: Mistaking ease of reading for real understanding

📖 References

  • Dunlosky, J. et al. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques. Psychological Science in the Public Interest.
  • Brown, P., Roediger, H. & McDaniel, M. (2014). Make It Stick. Harvard University Press.

quiz.q: A medical student in Buea makes 400 AI-generated Anki cards from one lecture. A friend curates 40 that test clinical decisions. Which outcome does the module predict?

The 400-card deck wins, because spaced repetition benefits scale with the number of reviews

quiz.q: A student scores 85% on AI-generated USMLE-style vignettes but 62% on a commercial question bank. What is the best interpretation?
opts: She should stop using AI questions, since they are clearly easier and add no value for the boards
The gap is random; averaging both scores gives the best estimate of her real level
AI items are good practice but imperfect calibrators; use the question bank for calibration
The commercial bank is outdated, so the AI score is the better estimate of exam readiness
quiz.x: AI-generated questions are good practice but difficulty drifts from real exams; use banks to calibrate. Abandoning AI questions discards useful volume.

quiz.q: A student wants AI vignettes that build discrimination skill rather than recognition. Which instruction is the core of the module's pedagogy?
opts: Ask for one-step recall questions so that facts are reinforced quickly and in volume
Ask for the hardest possible questions so that exam day feels comparatively easy
Ask for explanations of why each option is right or wrong, not just the correct answer

quiz.x: Explanation-for-every-option is the pedagogy: the wrong-answer autopsy builds discrimination. Maximum difficulty is plausible but not what builds discrimination.

Scores for organisation, red-flag coverage and empathy, plus the three questions she missed
A rating of her medical vocabulary compared with a qualified physician
A full transcript of the interview so she can review it later with a tutor or a classmate
quiz.x: The prompt asks for scores on organisation, red flags and empathy and the missed questions. The diagnosis matters but without the missed questions she learns little about history-taking.

Invitation
Knowledge
Perception
quiz.x: Perception assesses what the person already understands. Invitation, the runner-up, asks how much they want to know.

quiz.q: A student explains renal tubular acidosis to the AI and asks it to interrupt at every gap. Which technique is this and why does it work?
opts: The Feynman inversion: teaching the machine exposes gaps re-reading conceals
Spaced repetition: reviewing just before forgetting strengthens retention
Active recall: answering cloze cards repeatedly locks in the definitions
The three-level ladder: explaining at three altitudes builds the full concept
quiz.x: Teaching the AI and being interrupted is the Feynman inversion. The ladder has the AI explain at three levels, the reverse direction.

quiz.q: A student feels she understands cardiac physiology after reading a lucid AI explanation, but fails a closed-book quiz the next day. What does the module call this risk?
opts: Distribution shift
Fluency illusion
Anchoring bias
Automation bias
quiz.x: Fluency illusion is mistaking a clear explanation for learning. Automation bias concerns over-trusting machine outputs in decisions, a related but different idea.

quiz.q: A student wants to use AI help on an assessed research essay. Her friend says a short disclosure line makes any use acceptable. What does the module say decides this?
opts: AI may be used for grammar alone, which is universally permitted by medical schools
AI use is fine if under 20% of the text is generated, the common academic threshold
Her school's rules govern, and Module 5 norms for AI transparency also apply
Disclosure alone is enough, since transparency is the main integrity requirement
quiz.x: AI on graded work follows the school's policy, full stop, plus Module 5 disclosure norms. Disclosure is necessary but not sufficient if policy forbids the use.

quiz.q: Two students prepare for OSCEs. One uses AI to practise more stations weekly; the other uses AI summaries to cut study hours in half. Which does the module endorse and why?
opts: The second, as long as the summaries come from a reputable, recent and well-tested model
The second, because efficient study frees time for clinical attachments
Both equally, since total learning depends on outcome rather than method
The first: use AI to practise more, since shortcuts in formation become bedside gaps
quiz.x: Use AI to practise more, never to practise less. Freeing time for clinical attachments sounds reasonable but substitutes for practice.

quiz.q: A student wants to understand a difficult concept at multiple depths. Which prompt applies the three-level ladder correctly?
opts: 'Explain it to a 12-year-old, a nursing student and an attending: same core truth, three altitudes'
'Quiz me three times on it at increasing difficulty and correct my errors bluntly'
'Give three textbook sources that explain it at beginner, intermediate and advanced levels, with page numbers'
'Explain it in three sentences, then three paragraphs, then three pages of detail'
quiz.x: The ladder explains the same truth to three audiences. Varying length changes detail but not altitude, so the second option is a near-miss.

facts.t: Learning techniques rated 'high utility' in a major review: practice testing and distributed practice.
facts.more: Dunlosky et al. (2013) rated re-reading and highlighting low utility. Active recall and spacing are the engine of the study system.

facts.t: SPIKES: Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Empathy, Strategy.
facts.more: A widely taught protocol for breaking bad news (Baile et al., 2000). AI role-play lets you rehearse it with no patient at risk.

facts.t: A curated 40-card deck beats a 400-card AI dump.
facts.more: Delete cards testing trivia; keep cards testing decisions. One wrong card reviewed 30 times becomes a wrong memory.

facts.t: Reading a clear explanation feels like understanding.
facts.more: Recognition is not recall. Answer or draw it yourself first, then ask AI to critique — the reverse order builds the illusion.
