modules.d: Devices, not chatbots: reading validation studies, questioning vendors, and the global-health frontier.
modules.body:
A different species of AI

Everything so far has been assistive text. This module is about regulated medical devices: algorithms cleared by the FDA and international counterparts, with defined intended uses, validation dossiers, and post-market obligations. Hundreds of such clearances now exist — roughly three-quarters in radiology — and the number compounds yearly. A clinician who can read a validation claim is worth ten who can repeat a headline.

Where cleared AI actually works today

  • Radiology triage: intracranial hemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, and pneumothorax flags that re-order the reading worklist — minutes saved on true emergencies, with the radiologist still reading everything.
  • Stroke coordination: platforms that detect large-vessel occlusion on CT angiography and alert the intervention team directly — among the best-evidenced time-to-treatment improvements in deployed clinical AI.
  • Mammography: AI-supported screening validated in large prospective European programs — maintained or improved detection with substantially reduced radiologist workload.
  • Ophthalmology: autonomous diabetic-retinopathy screening at point of care — historic as the first autonomous AI diagnostic clearance, extending screening to clinics with no ophthalmologist.
  • Cardiology: ECG algorithms flagging low-EF and arrhythmia risk from routine tracings; smartwatch AF detection pushing rhythm screening into daily life (with a real conversation to have about false positives in low-risk populations).
  • Pathology: cleared digital-pathology assistants for prostate biopsy review and mitosis counting — the microscope’s turn.

How to read a validation claim (the core skill)

  • Population: validated on whom? Age, ethnicity, scanner types, disease prevalence. Performance does not travel automatically — the distribution-shift lesson from Module 1, now with regulatory stakes.
  • Metrics at YOUR prevalence: sensitivity/specificity are prevalence-independent, but positive predictive value collapses in low-prevalence settings. A 95%-sensitive, 90%-specific tool screening a 1%-prevalence population generates ~10 false alarms per true case. Do this arithmetic before every deployment conversation.
  • Ground truth: against what standard was it measured — expert consensus, biopsy, outcomes? Weak ground truth inflates claims.
  • Prospective vs retrospective: retrospective excellence routinely shrinks in prospective deployment; ask which one the claim rests on.

The five vendor questions (bring these to every demo)

  • 1. What is your validation population, and how does it differ from mine?
  • 2. Sensitivity, specificity — and PPV at MY prevalence?
  • 3. How does it integrate into workflow, and what happens when it is down?
  • 4. Who bears liability for algorithm-influenced misses, and what does my insurer say?
  • 5. What is the post-deployment monitoring plan for drift, and who watches it?

The global-health frontier

The most consequential deployments may be where specialists are scarcest: WHO now conditionally recommends computer-aided detection for TB screening on chest radiographs in settings without radiologists; retinopathy screening runs in primary-care clinics; AI-guided ultrasound lets minimally trained operators acquire diagnostic-quality cardiac and obstetric images. Evaluate these with the same five questions PLUS the field realities: connectivity, power, maintenance, and local validation — a tool validated in London serving Lagos deserves Lagos validation.

Patients arrive pre-briefed

Your patients consult chatbots before consulting you. The productive script: acknowledge ("good that you’re researching"), correct specifically (not "don’t Google" but "here’s what that source missed about your case"), and redirect to sources you trust. The clinician who engages the AI-informed patient keeps the relationship; the one who scoffs loses it.

🧪 Interactive Lab — the PPV reality check

Act as a biostatistics tutor. Walk me through positive and negative predictive value step by step for a screening AI with sensitivity [95]% and specificity [90]% at disease prevalences of 1%, 5%, and 20%. Show the 2x2 tables, the false-alarms-per-true-case ratio at each prevalence, and then explain in two paragraphs — suitable for a department meeting — why an impressive tool can still flood a low-prevalence clinic with false positives, and what deployment choices mitigate it.

Going deeper — reading a validation claim

When a vendor says "98% accurate", ask what was measured and on whom. Key concepts:

  • Sensitivity and specificity describe the test; positive predictive value (PPV) depends on prevalence. Worked example: a tool with 95% sensitivity and 95% specificity, used where prevalence is 1%, in 10,000 scans finds 95 of 100 true cases but also flags 495 false positives (5% of 9,900). PPV = 95 ÷ 590 ≈ 16%. Most alerts are false — at a prevalence where the brochure looked superb.
  • External validation: was the model tested on data from other hospitals, scanners and populations, not just the development site? Performance commonly drops on external data.
  • Intended use: regulatory clearance applies to a defined use (e.g. triage prioritisation of suspected intracranial haemorrhage), population and setting. Using it outside that scope is off-label.
  • Post-market monitoring and drift: performance can change with new scanners, protocols or populations. Ask how the vendor and your department will monitor it.
Regulatory landscape: in the US, most AI devices reach market through 510(k) clearance; the FDA has also finalised guidance on predetermined change control plans for AI-enabled devices. In the EU, AI medical devices fall under the MDR and are generally classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act, with obligations phasing in through 2026–2027. Check current timelines.
🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a clinical AI evaluator. Here is a vendor's validation summary: [paste]. Calculate PPV and NPV at our prevalence of [x]%, identify whether validation was external, state the intended use and any off-label risks in our setting, and list five questions to ask the vendor about monitoring and drift.

📚 Glossary

  • Sensitivity: Proportion of true cases a test detects
  • Specificity: Proportion of non-cases correctly identified
  • PPV: Probability that a positive result is truly positive; depends on prevalence
  • External validation: Testing a model on data from settings other than where it was developed
  • Intended use: The specific purpose and population a device is cleared for

📖 References

  • U.S. FDA — Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices list and PCCP guidance (2024).
  • Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) and Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR).

quiz.q: An AI screening tool has 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. It is used in a population with 1% prevalence. About how many false alarms occur per true case detected?

About 5
About 100
About 10
quiz.x: Per 10,000: 95 true positives and 990 false positives (10% of 9,900), so about 10 false alarms per true case; PPV is about 9%.

quiz.q: The same tool (95% sensitivity, 90% specificity) is moved to a referral clinic with 20% prevalence. What happens to the positive predictive value?
opts: It rises to roughly 70%, because more of the positives are true cases
It stays near 9%, since sensitivity and specificity are unchanged
It falls, because higher prevalence produces more false positives
It rises to about 95%, matching the sensitivity of the tool
quiz.x: Per 10,000: 1,900 TP and 800 FP, so PPV is about 70%. Sensitivity and specificity are prevalence-independent; PPV is not.

quiz.q: A vendor in Lagos claims '98% accurate' for a TB chest X-ray tool, validated retrospectively in London. Which of the five vendor questions should come first?
opts: Who bears liability for algorithm-influenced misses, and what does the insurer say?
How does it integrate into workflow, and what happens when it is down?
What is the validation population, and how does it differ from ours?
What is the post-deployment monitoring plan for drift, and who watches it?
quiz.x: Performance does not travel automatically; a London-validated tool serving Lagos deserves local validation. The others matter but depend on whether the tool works here at all.

opts: WHO recommends CAD in high-income settings with radiologist oversight
WHO conditionally recommends CAD for TB screening on chest X-rays in such settings
WHO prohibits AI for TB screening until local trials are completed
WHO recommends CAD to replace sputum testing for TB diagnosis in all settings
quiz.x: WHO conditionally recommends CAD for TB screening where radiologists are lacking. It is screening, not a replacement for bacteriological confirmation.

quiz.q: A stroke centre in Atlanta debates which deployed AI has the best evidence for time-to-treatment improvement. Which category does the module highlight?
opts: Smartwatch atrial fibrillation detection pushing rhythm screening into daily life

quiz.x: LVO detection platforms are among the best-evidenced time-to-treatment improvements. Mammography has strong evidence too, but for workload and detection, not time to treatment.

quiz.q: An autonomous diabetic-retinopathy screener is placed in a Bamenda primary care clinic without an eye doctor. Why is this category historically significant?
opts: It was the first autonomous AI diagnostic clearance, allowing screening without a specialist
It was the first AI diagnostic tool validated prospectively in sub-Saharan African clinics
It was the first imaging AI to replace fundus photography with smartphone images
It was the first AI system approved to prescribe treatment without physician review
quiz.x: Autonomous DR screening was the first autonomous AI diagnostic clearance. It does not prescribe treatment; referral follows a positive screen.

quiz.q: A vendor's pneumothorax tool showed excellent results in a retrospective dataset. A radiology chair asks what to expect in prospective deployment. What is the best answer?
opts: Unknown, so the tool should not be deployed before a randomised trial is completed
Better performance, as radiologists will correct the tool's errors in real time

Possibly weaker performance, since retrospective excellence often shrinks prospectively
quiz.x: Retrospective excellence routinely shrinks prospectively; ask which one the claim rests on. Requiring an RCT for every tool is an overcorrection.

quiz.q: A tool's accuracy was measured against a single radiologist's reads rather than biopsy or outcomes. What concern does this raise?
opts: Sensitivity will be overstated, but specificity will be accurate

quiz.x: Ground truth determines what accuracy means; weak reference standards inflate claims. Distribution shift is real but concerns a different question.

quiz.x: Acknowledge, correct specifically and redirect; scoffing loses the relationship. Ordering a full panel is defensive medicine that does not address her understanding.

Connectivity, power, maintenance and local validation

facts.t: The FDA authorised the first autonomous AI diagnostic system: diabetic-retinopathy screening (IDx-DR).

facts.t: WHO recommends computer-aided detection to read chest X-rays for TB screening.
facts.more: WHO's 2021 screening guidance allows CAD in place of human readers for people aged 15+, especially where radiologists are scarce. Local validation still matters.

modules.t: Capstone: Your Clinical AI Workflow & Governance Note
modules.d: Two weeks of measured deployment, a policy your department could adopt, and the presentation that proves it.
modules.body:
What this capstone is — and is not

This is not an essay. It is a deployment: one AI-augmented workflow running in your real professional life for two measured weeks, wrapped in the governance thinking that would let your department adopt it tomorrow. Graduates have used this exact artifact to become their institution’s AI lead, to win pilot funding, and — in one memorable case — to talk a hospital out of a bad vendor contract.

Component 1 — The workflow (choose one, go deep)

  • Documentation: a scribe or structured-note pipeline (Modules 2–3) across ≥20 encounters.
  • Patient education: a literacy-tiered, bilingual instruction system for your three commonest discharge scenarios.
  • Study OS: the full Module 6 machine, run for two weeks with score data (students).
  • Research pipeline: the Module 5 mini-review executed end to end.
  • Evidence workflow: a foreground-question routine using the Module 4 stack, logged across two weeks of real questions.

Component 2 — The measurement (numbers, honestly)

  • Time: baseline vs deployed, measured not estimated (note-completion minutes, questions-answered-per-hour, cards-per-lecture — whatever fits your workflow).
  • Quality: a defined check (edits per note, verification failures caught, score movement, mentor-rated samples).
  • The error log: your five most instructive AI failures from the fortnight, categorized (factual / inferential / omission / tone), each with how you caught it. Examiners read this section first — it is where judgment shows.

Component 3 — The governance note (one page, adoptable)

  • Data rules: which data classes may enter which tools (your Module 2 green/amber/red paths, made local).
  • Approved tools & verification standard: named tools, the 60-second rule operationalized, citation-opening policy.
  • Disclosure: to patients (scribes/consent), in documentation, in academic work.
  • Review cadence: who re-examines this policy, how often, and what triggers early review (new tool, incident, guideline change). Model it on WHO’s six principles — autonomy, safety, transparency, accountability, equity, sustainability — and say so; reviewers upstream of you will recognize the scaffold.

Component 4 — The tool matrix

Your Modules 3–4 selection matrices completed with CURRENT verified pricing and terms for your context — the perishable homework that proves you can re-do it whenever the market moves.

Component 5 — The presentation

Ten minutes to the mentor panel, structured as if to your department: the problem, the workflow, the numbers, the failures and catches, the governance ask. Then ten minutes of adversarial questions — expect the PPV arithmetic, the liability question, and "what breaks first at scale?"

Grading rubric: deployment reality (30%) · measurement honesty (25%) · error-log insight (20%) · governance adoptability (15%) · presentation under fire (10%). Pass mark 70%. Distinction earns the right to mentor next cohort’s medical track.
Certification: completing all module quizzes (≥70% each) and the capstone earns the AI Unlocked: Medicine certificate, printable from your Certificates tab, signed by Innocent Forteh, Program Manager. Continue with AI in Public Health for population-scale applications, or Level 2: OPERATE to automate what you built here.

Going deeper — writing a governance note leadership can approve

A strong governance note follows the structure that clinical governance committees already use, adapted for AI. Draw on the WHO's guidance on the ethics and governance of AI for health and on recognised reporting frameworks.

  • Purpose and scope: the problem, the workflow, who uses the tool, which patients, and what it must not be used for.
  • Data and privacy: what data flows where, legal basis, contracts (BAA/DPA), retention and access.
  • Safety case: known failure modes, how errors will be detected (review rules, audits), and an incident reporting route.
  • Equity: which patient groups could be disadvantaged (language, disability, digital access), and how you'll monitor.
  • Evaluation: baseline and after measures, a minimum sample, and a stop rule.
  • Accountability: named clinical owner, review date, and training requirements.
Reporting frameworks to know: DECIDE-AI for early-stage clinical evaluation of AI decision support, CONSORT-AI and SPIRIT-AI for trials, and TRIPOD+AI for prediction models. Citing them signals rigour to committees and journals.

Measuring your two-week pilot honestly

Record a baseline week before the AI (e.g. after-hours charting minutes), then the pilot weeks. Log every AI error you catch. Report both benefits and problems; a governance note that reports none of the latter won't be believed.

🧪 Interactive Lab — try it now

You are a clinical governance committee chair. Here is my AI workflow and pilot data: [paste]. Review it against WHO AI-for-health principles: purpose and scope, data and privacy, safety case, equity, evaluation and accountability. Identify the three weakest sections, ask me the questions the committee would ask, and suggest a stop rule.

📚 Glossary

  • Governance note: Document setting out how an AI use is controlled, monitored and owned
  • Stop rule: Pre-agreed condition under which a pilot is halted
  • DECIDE-AI: Reporting guideline for early clinical evaluation of AI decision support
  • TRIPOD+AI: Reporting guideline for prediction models using AI

📖 References

  • WHO (2021). Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health; WHO (2024) guidance on large multi-modal models.
  • Vasey, B. et al. (2022). DECIDE-AI reporting guideline. Nature Medicine.
  • Collins, G.S. et al. (2024). TRIPOD+AI statement. BMJ.

quiz.q: A GP in Kumba plans to report her scribe pilot's time savings. Which measurement approach meets the capstone's standard for honesty?
opts: Record a baseline week of note-completion minutes, then measure pilot weeks identically
Survey colleagues for their impression of how much time she saved
Estimate minutes saved per day from memory at the end of the two weeks
Use the vendor's published average time savings for clinicians in her specialty
quiz.x: Time must be measured, not estimated: baseline vs deployed. Vendor averages are the runner-up but describe other clinicians, not her workflow.

quiz.q: Examiners read one capstone section first because it shows clinical judgement. Which is it?
opts: The tool matrix with current, verified pricing and contract terms
The time-savings measurement with baseline comparisons
The error log of the five most instructive AI failures
The governance note with data rules and review cadence
quiz.x: The error log is read first because it shows judgement. The governance note is important but weighted less and read later.

quiz.q: A capstone error log lists an entry: the scribe recorded the patient's own quoted words as a statement made by the doctor. Which of the capstone's error categories fits best?
opts: Inferential: the note draws a wrong conclusion from true facts
Factual: the note states something untrue about who said what
Omission: the note leaves out a relevant finding or statement
Tone: the note's wording is inappropriate for the medical record
quiz.x: Misattribution records an untrue fact about the encounter, so it is factual. Inferential is the runner-up but applies when facts are right and the conclusion drawn is wrong.

quiz.q: A department head asks which WHO principles should scaffold the governance note. Which list matches the module?
opts: Autonomy, safety, transparency, accountability, equity, sustainability
Validity, reliability, fairness, explainability, robustness, auditability
Beneficence, non-maleficence, justice, autonomy, fidelity, veracity
Privacy, consent, security, accuracy, efficiency, interoperability
quiz.x: WHO's six principles are autonomy, safety, transparency, accountability, equity and sustainability. The second list is classical bioethics, a plausible confusion.

quiz.q: A capstone candidate in Bafoussam must decide where to spend her limited remaining time. Under the module's grading rubric, which component carries the most weight in the final mark?
opts: Measurement honesty at 25%
Error-log insight at 20%
Deployment reality at 30%
Governance adoptability at 15%
quiz.x: Deployment reality is 30%, then measurement honesty 25%, error log 20%, governance 15% and presentation 10%.

quiz.q: A capstone student planning an early-stage evaluation of an AI decision-support tool in her ward wants a recognised reporting framework. Which fits best?
opts: CONSORT-AI, for randomised trials of AI interventions
TRIPOD+AI, for development and validation of prediction models
SPIRIT-AI, for protocols of clinical trials involving AI interventions
DECIDE-AI, built for first-in-clinic studies of AI that guides decisions
quiz.x: DECIDE-AI covers early-stage clinical evaluation of decision support. CONSORT-AI is for trials, a later stage.

quiz.q: A governance note says 'policy will be reviewed as needed.' What improvement does the module require?
opts: Assign review to the vendor, since it knows the tool's updates best
Name who reviews, how often, and what triggers early review (new tool, incident, new guideline)
Commit to monthly reviews by an external consultant to ensure independence from the department
Remove the review clause, since policies should remain stable once approved
quiz.x: Review cadence names who, how often and early triggers. Monthly external review is specific but costly and lacks triggers.

quiz.q: A capstone pilot shows note-completion time fell 40%, but edits per note doubled. How should the student present this?
opts: Report the time savings as the headline and omit the edit data as secondary
Discard the pilot, since any rise in edits shows the tool is unsafe
Report both, analyse why edits rose, and decide whether quality is acceptable
Report the edit data as the headline, since quality outweighs speed in every clinical setting
quiz.x: Measurement honesty requires both time and quality metrics. Discarding the pilot overreacts without analysing the edits.

quiz.q: During the adversarial questions, a mentor asks 'what breaks first at scale?' about a scribe workflow used by one doctor. What answer shows the best governance thinking?
opts: Nothing, since a workflow that worked for one doctor will work for all
The model will degrade, so the workflow should be retrained monthly
Costs rise steeply, so the department should negotiate a volume discount before expanding
Copy-paste integration, consent workflows and IT support become bottlenecks as users multiply
quiz.x: Copy-paste is fine solo but fails at clinic scale, and consent and support processes must scale too. Cost matters but is not what breaks first.

quiz.q: A clinic's draft governance note for an AI scribe has a blank equity section. What content does the module expect there before a committee could approve it?
opts: Groups who could be disadvantaged (language, disability, digital access) and how to monitor
A statement that the tool treats all patients identically
A commitment to offer the tool free of charge to low-income and uninsured patients at the clinic
A list of the demographic groups in the vendor's training dataset
quiz.x: The equity section names who could be disadvantaged and how it will be monitored. Vendor training demographics help but do not address monitoring in your patients.

facts.t: Weight of 'deployment reality' in the capstone rubric — the largest single criterion.
facts.more: Then measurement honesty 25%, error-log insight 20%, governance adoptability 15%, presentation 10%. Pass mark 70%.

facts.t: Reporting guideline for early-stage clinical evaluation of AI decision support.
facts.more: Published in Nature Medicine in 2022. Citing it signals rigour to governance committees and journals.

facts.t: Reporting guideline for prediction models that use AI or machine learning.
facts.more: Published in the BMJ in 2024, updating TRIPOD 2015. CONSORT-AI and SPIRIT-AI cover trials.

facts.t: A pre-agreed condition under which a pilot is halted.
facts.more: For example: any fabricated exam finding reaching a signed note, or edit time above baseline for two weeks. Committees trust pilots that can stop themselves.

plaibox.title: Simulation: the governance committee

steps.s: 'Who is accountable if an AI fabrication reaches a chart?'

Right — signature means ownership; a named owner governs the tool.
The vendor, under the liability terms of the contract
No AI or vendor holds a licence for your patient's care.

steps.s: The committee asks for one change before approving.
